newsitem.title: USA: Suzuki says Consumer Reports rigged swerve test.
newsitem.headline: Suzuki says Consumer Reports rigged swerve test.

text.p: Suzuki Motor Corp. Tuesday escalated its feud with Consumers Union, claiming that its once popular Samurai sports-utility vehicle was set up to fail in a flawed 1988 swerve test conducted by the group.

The Japanese car maker's U.S. subsidiary, American Suzuki Motor Corp., offered evidence, including videotape and the testimony of a former Consumers Union employee, that it said shows that the group set out to make the Samurai fail.

"This shows that the object of Consumers Union tests was not to test the vehicle fairly, but instead to make it roll over for the cameras," American Suzuki General Counsel George Ball told a news conference.
After the test, Consumers Union reported in its Consumer Reports magazine that the Samurai was prone to rollovers. Suzuki said the report caused its 1989 sales to plummet.
Consumers Union, which is based in Yonkers, N.Y., has defended the integrity of its testing procedures.

American Suzuki, which is based in Brea, Calif., has long claimed that the swerve tests were flawed. Extreme steering and other procedures used exceed the conditions of avoidance in normal driving, it has said.

Its new claim, however, is that Consumers Union officials rigged the 1988 test to make the Samurai tip on two wheels in an effort to boost the sales of its magazine by slamming what was then a new and hot-selling recreational vehicle.
"I submit they took on the Suzuki Samurai in part because you had a new kid on the block," said Ball.
It said it asked the National Highway Traffic Safety Admininitration to investigate Consumers Union's testing.

Suzuki released test logs from two different drivers, with one saying the vehicle "rocks a bit but never felt like it would tip over," and the other saying it responds well, corrects quickly and has "no real problem."

An affidavit of former Consumers Union technician Ronald Denison released by Suzuki claimed that Consumers Union Editorial Director Irwin Landau interceded in the test and told one of the drivers in a loud voice, "If you can't find someone to roll this car, I will."
Ball admitted, however, after repeated questioning, that Denison was terminated by Consumers Union over a "difference of opinion." Denison declined to talk to reporters.

The company issued a videotape in which testing personnel can be heard laughing and cheering after an executive who it said does not usually test drive vehicles made the Samurai tip on two wheels on its 47th run through an obstacle course.

It said the videotape, obtained in the course of a lawsuit the company filed against Consumers Union last April, shows that the vehicle was then put through a new, more demanding test in which it took drivers 15 attempts to get it to tip.

Consumers Union, noting that a U.S. District Court judge in California threw out nearly all of the charges in the libel and product disparagement suit two months ago, said its testing producedures were scientifically sound.
"The CU test is dependable, it's reliable and the American public has a right to know what cars might tip up," said attorney James Fitzpatrick who represents Consumers Union.
Fitzpatrick, who called the evidence issued by Suzuki "an attempt to resuscitate their position," said that the Samurai was one of only two vehicles that failed the test out of 57 that were tested.
